record.title: A preprint measures the limits of generic OS defenses for self-hosted agent state
record.summary: Chen, Denis, Di Pietro and Schmidhuber define self-state attacks as corruption of an agent’s persistent memory, instructions or configuration through the agent’s own authorized host writes. Their arXiv v2 paper evaluates prevention, detection, provenance and recovery on one Linux reference backend with four contrastive workloads. It reports that broad generic detectors catch many attacks but trigger on substantial legitimate activity, while selective write-specific detectors apply to only 23 of 55 admitted attacks. Full barriers stop all six tested file mutations but also reject the paired authorized update. Protected backups restore all tested corruptions only when held beyond the compromised principal’s reach; choosing a trustworthy recovery point and limiting rollback loss remain open. The paper does not establish these tradeoffs across production deployments or other operating systems.
organizations: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors define self-state attacks as malicious corruption of agent memory, instructions or configuration through host operations that use the agent’s legitimate authorization, and organize the attack space across target, mutation mechanism, edit granularity and timing.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the authors’ 55-attack / 60-natural-execution evaluation, broad detector baselines cover most or all attacks but produce substantial natural-workload positives; write-specific methods produce fewer natural positives but are evaluable on only 23 of 55 attacks.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a six-operation replay on one durable-memory object, the tested immutable-file, AppArmor and Landlock configurations blocked all six replayed mutation paths and also rejected the corresponding approved direct update.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Protected backup storage survived same-principal backup destruction and restored all tested corruptions, while recovery still depends on selecting a trustworthy point and can roll back legitimate updates.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The reported empirical design uses one Linux reference backend and four contrastive workload profiles, not a representative sample of deployed self-hosted agents; 20 of the 55 attack executions are directly instantiated under the compromised agent principal rather than induced end-to-end by a model.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent team has reproduced the detector, prevention or recovery results; code and derived artifacts are not yet available in the inspected version, and raw telemetry is excluded.
Generality beyond the single Linux reference backend and four contrastive workload regimes is unmeasured; the workloads are not a probability sample of deployments.
The paper’s result motivates a self-state-aware update boundary but does not implement or evaluate which combination of task context, state role or update phase achieves adequate selectivity.

brief.importance_rationale: If the scoped findings hold across representative self-hosted agent deployments, generic host-level controls alone may not distinguish malicious writes to behavior-governing state from authorized updates, affecting practical agent-security architecture. The paper does not establish prevalence or generality beyond its Linux testbed.
limitations: All performance and defense outcomes are author-reported; no independent reproduction was performed.
The 55-attack corpus combines 35 model-driven persistent-write cases with 20 attacks instantiated directly under the compromised principal; it does not show that every case is model-inducible.
The 60 held-out natural executions span 20 scenarios; profile-level rates from five scenarios are descriptive, not deployment prevalence estimates.

The main live results use one Linux reference backend. Cross-platform expectations are discussion, not measured results. Prevention replay covers six operations against one MEMORY.md object and is not a proof over all Linux authority paths or policy designs.
Artifacts are described as forthcoming upon paper acceptance; raw telemetry is excluded and no external code or independent result reproduction was available in this review.

brief.summary: Chen, Denis, Di Pietro and Schmidhuber define self-state attacks as corruption of an agent’s persistent memory, instructions or configuration through the agent’s own authorized host writes. Their arXiv v2 paper evaluates prevention, detection, provenance and recovery on one Linux reference backend with four contrastive workloads. It reports that broad generic detectors catch many attacks but trigger on substantial legitimate activity, while selective write-specific detectors apply to only 23 of 55 admitted attacks. Full barriers stop all six tested file mutations but also reject the paired authorized update. Protected backups restore all tested corruptions only when held beyond the compromised principal’s reach; choosing a trustworthy recovery point and limiting rollback loss remain open. The paper does not establish these tradeoffs across production deployments or other operating systems.

technical.claimed_result: The paper reports 55 adjudicated attack executions and 60 held-out natural executions from 20 scenarios. AIDE covered 55/55 attacks with 32/60 natural positives; Falco 55/55 with 21/60; STIDE 55/55 with 58/60. Write-specific B1/B2 and supervised methods covered only 23/55 attacks, with natural positives ranging from 3/60 to 10/60. In a separate six-operation replay on MEMORY.md, immutable files, AppArmor and Landlock blocked all six tested mutations but also blocked the paired authorized direct update. Protected storage restored all eight supplemental corruptions and survived same-principal backup destruction. These figures are author-reported.
technical.compute_or_cost: Not a model-training or inference-cost study. The main pipeline runs isolated Linux VMs; the paper specifies per-process resource limits but does not estimate deployment cost.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected arXiv v2 paper documents its threat model, four contrastive workloads, admitted populations, Linux telemetry pipeline, detector definitions and reported outcomes. Those manuscript details establish what the authors report and the bounded experimental design; no result was independently reproduced in this review.
technical.implementation_status: Preprint v2 revised 2026-09-17. Authors state code and derived artifact files will be released with a permanent Zenodo identifier upon acceptance; no such artifact was available from the inspected paper. Raw telemetry is excluded.
technical.mechanism: The authors define self-state as persistent agent memory, instructions and configuration that can shape later decisions. After assuming an agent has already been compromised through untrusted input, they evaluate generic OS file controls, integrity and syscall detectors, provenance signals, statistical/supervised write detectors, and protected backups. The measured question is whether host-operation features can cover attacker-induced mutations while preserving legitimate self-state changes.
technical.novelty: The work centers the agent’s behavior-governing self-state as a distinct OS security target and evaluates attack coverage, selectivity on legitimate writes and recovery exposure together. Its contribution is the measured tradeoff and benchmark design, not a demonstrated defense that resolves it.
technical.regime: One Linux 6.8.0 x86-64 reference backend for the main five-source corpus, with four contrastive workload profiles. The admitted attack population contains 35 model-driven persistent writes and 20 direct post-compromise metadata/namespace mutations; held-out natural activity contains 60 executions across 20 scenarios. Prevention replays cover six operations against one MEMORY.md object; recovery and platform portability are scoped separately.
technical.reproducibility: The paper provides detailed protocols, frozen populations and baseline definitions, and says derived result JSON/manifests are planned for Zenodo upon acceptance. The raw telemetry is excluded; recalculation from raw events or full pipeline reruns require unreleased telemetry or privileged Linux infrastructure and model credentials. No independent reproduction was performed.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within the paper, the broadest detector baselines (AIDE, Falco, STIDE) have 55/55 attack coverage, but natural positive rates from 21/60 to 58/60; the more selective write-specific methods lower natural positives but are defined on only 23/55 attacks. The study does not compare a self-state-aware context mechanism.

brief.title: A preprint measures the limits of generic OS defenses for self-hosted agent state
brief.why_it_matters: Self-hosted agents can write files that shape their future behavior, so ordinary filesystem permission and telemetry controls may not distinguish an authorized memory update from a malicious one after the agent is compromised. If the paper’s scoped measurements hold more broadly, defenses need a separate, context-aware update boundary alongside isolation and protected recovery.
